quote: Es [-sch-] scheint dass auch [-da-] im allgemeinsten Falle $f(x,\lambda)$ für gewisse $\lambda$ und alle $x$ singulär ist?
english: It seems that even in the most general case f(x,λ) is singular for certain λ and all x?
topic: Hilbert discusses the dependence of solutions of differential equations on a parameter λ, noting that they have poles at the special values of λ, and asks general questions about singularities and branching in the parameter and about whether the coefficient A(x) is determined by the singular values.

triage.modern_statement: Take a linear ODE (for example a Sturm–Liouville-type equation with coefficient A(x)) that depends analytically on a spectral parameter λ. Let f(x,λ) be the solution normalised by boundary conditions, or equivalently the Green's function/resolvent. Hilbert asks whether, in complete generality, the singularities of f in λ always occur at a discrete set of special λ (the eigenvalues), and whether at each such λ the function is singular for every x, i.e. it has poles in λ whose location does not depend on x. In modern terms: is the resolvent (λ-dependent boundary-value solution) a meromorphic function of λ whose poles are the eigenvalues, the same for all x? The companion question on the page, whether A(x) is determined by the singular values, is the inverse spectral problem.
triage.answered_by: My searches did not pin this note to a specific later paper; the attribution here is my inference. The analytic structure Hilbert guessed became standard theory. Poincaré had shown that solutions of initial-value problems are analytic in the parameters (entire in λ for linear equations). The Fredholm (1903) and Hilbert (1904–1910) theory of integral equations then showed that the resolvent of a boundary-value problem is a ratio of entire functions of λ (the Fredholm determinant in the denominator), so it is meromorphic in λ with poles exactly at the eigenvalues, independent of x. I could not confirm this Fredholm/Hilbert result with a source because the search limit ran out. The related question of whether A(x) is fixed by the singular values was taken up by Ambarzumian (1929). Borg (1946) proved that one spectrum is not enough in general but two spectra determine the potential uniquely; Gelfand–Levitan and Marchenko followed (not checked against a source).

evidence.claim: Poincaré's theorem: solutions of differential equations are analytic functions of the initial conditions and of parameters, under analyticity hypotheses on the right-hand side.

Modern theory treats meromorphic operator functions with Fredholm values (Keldysh's theorem), where the eigenvalues are the poles of the resolvent. This is the general form of 'singular for certain λ'.
Inverse spectral theory goes back at least to Ambarzumian in 1929, who studied recovering the potential of a Sturm–Liouville operator from its spectrum.
Borg (1946) proved that two spectra of a Sturm–Liouville equation uniquely determine the potential.
Borg showed that one spectrum does not determine the potential in general, so two spectra are needed.

triage.why: The note is short and gives no explicit equation, so linking it to the resolvent and spectral theory is my interpretation. On that reading, the analytic part (poles in λ at the eigenvalues, the same for all x) became classical through Poincaré and Fredholm–Hilbert theory. The Fredholm/Hilbert attribution is from memory and was not confirmed by any source found. The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The basic question is settled. The companion question about determining A(x) from the singular values grew into inverse spectral theory (Ambarzumian 1929, Borg 1946), which is still a research area, but the narrow question in this note is not.
